an2.55:1.1: Four such are mentioned at [an4.247:1.4]() and [dn16:5.12.1](). A Queen receives a monument at [an5.50:19.2](), and the monk Bāhiya at [ud1.10:11.3](). | The “monument” (_thūpa_) is mentioned rarely in the Suttas (), but became a major feature of the Buddhist landscape. Buddhist monuments were round in shape, which was apparently a characteristic of the lands around Magadha. Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.8.1.5 says that the correct form of such a monument was square, and that round monuments were built by godless “easterners”.
an2.56:1.3: “Independent Buddhas” are sages who discover the Dhamma and are awakened independently, but who do not themselves go on to found a dispensation or establish a monastic order. For more details, see [mn116]() and notes there.
an2.60:1.1: The nature of the “mystery man” (_kiṁpurisa_, literally, “what man?”) is not entirely clear. He appears as a substitute in the human sacrifice (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.3.9, 7.5.2.32, Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.1), in which case it could be an effigy or perhaps a primate of some kind. The context here assumes that the lack of common speech by _kiṁpurisa_ requires explanation. Thus a _kiṁpurisa_ may be a tribal person or aboriginal whose speech was incomprehensible. On the other hand, later Buddhist tradition treats the mystery man as a shy denizen of the deep forest, a beguiling “pixie” ([thig14.1:10.4]()). | Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa treats _mānusiṁ vācaṁ_ as “common speech” in contrast with the divine words of the Vedas (1.1.4.9, 1.7.4.21, 3.2.2.29, 3.5.4.17, 4.6.9.19, 5.4.4.14, 10.5.1.1).
an2.60:1.3: This suggests that they adhere to a primitive or naive purity in contrast with the decadent and untrustworthy society of man. Buddhist myths depict lying as emerging only at a late stage of societal decline ([dn26:14.8]()).
an2.61:1.1: _Mātugāma_ (“lady”) literally means “motherkind” (cf. the archaic “motherkin”). It is a word for women in Pali, but it appears unique to Buddhist texts, and hence may be a technical or formal term (cf. _puggala_, [sn22.22:2.2]()). Grammatically it is always singular, but it sometimes takes a plural sense as a collective noun. At [sn37.1:1.1](), for example, _mātugāma_ is paired with “man” so it must be a singular “woman”, whereas at [sn37.3:1.1]() it is paired with “men” in plural so it must be “womankind”. In the current Sutta, the use of the third person present shows that it is meant as a general statement, rather than referring to a particular woman. The commentary says _mātugāma_ refers to any female human, even one born that very day. As to the connotations, “mother” is probably meant in an affectionate and respectful sense, perhaps to remind the monks not to fall into objectification (cf. [sn35.127:1.6]()). There are different patterns of usage in different texts. Throughout the Pātimokkha—the quintessential text for monks—_mātugāma_ is used with _bhikkhu_, whereas _itthī_ (“woman”) is used with _purisa_ (“man”). But there is no corresponding male form, so _bhikkhunī_ takes _purisa_. However, this distinction does not obtain in the Suttas, where _mātugāma_ is used with _purisa_. Overall, I think _mātugāma_ is respectful and slightly formal, so I use “lady” for _mātugāma_ and “woman” for _itthī_.
an2.61:1.4: This is the first of several discourses in the Aṅguttara Nikāya that launch seemingly unmotivated and baseless attacks on women, without criticizing men in comparable ways, such as the failings of women at [an4.80](), the “black snake” discourses at [an5.229]() and [an5.230](), and the ordination of women at [an8.51](). Such passages should be interrogated in light of the four factors of right speech. First of all, is it true? While it is true that some women like having many children, the claim here is that women generally want to be continually giving birth until they die. Giving birth is, of course, extremely painful and dangerous, and I have never heard of a single woman who expressed such a wish. Is it pleasing to the ear? Not to me, and when I share such teachings with students I am yet to find anyone who finds them inspiring and uplifting. Is it harmonious, leading to the reconciling of divisions? On the contrary, statements like this exacerbate bigotry and fuel disdain between people based on sex and gender. Finally, is it meaningful? Does it lead to the goal of ending greed, hate, and delusion? I don’t see how this can be, and in thirty years as a monk I have not heard of a single person who has been helped in their path by such teachings. My conclusion is that this passage fails not just one, but all four of the factors of right speech, and therefore cannot have been spoken by the Buddha. As to how such things appear in the canon, notice that this is a short passage with no context. Elsewhere, the contextualization of such passages was contested in the Buddhist tradition, leading to radically different perspectives ([an5.229]()).
an2.63:1.1: Text reads _vacīsaṁsāro_ (“incessant discussion”), while at [mn103:15.1]() we find variants _vacīsaṁhāro_ (“speech accumulation”), and _vacīsaṅkhāro_ (“speech activity”). The commentary to MN glosses with _vacanasañcāro_ (“wandering talk”), while the subcommentary here has _pavattamānā_ (“rolling on”), both of which support the dominant reading _vacīsaṁsāro_. Their explanations differ, however, as the MN commentary explains as spreading rumors from one place to another, while here it is said to be ongoing arguing. Since the normal meaning of _saṁsāra_ is “endless ongoing”, and since, in both MN and AN, this follows a passage where disputes were supposed to have been settled, perhaps the sense is “continuing to bring up matters that have been settled”.
